title: E. Zero Trailing Factorial
statement:
For all positive integers $$x$\geq 1$$$ and $$k$\geq 2$$$, let $$v_k(x!)$$ denote the number of trailing zeros in the base-$$k$$ representation of $$x! = x$\cdot (x-1)\cdot \ldots \cdot 1$$$. Formally, $$v_k(x!)$$ is defined as the largest integer $$i$$ such that $$k^i$$ divides $$x!$$.

For a prime number $$p$$, we can calculate $$v_p(x!) = $\sum\limits_{j=1}^\infty \left\lfloor \frac{x}{p^j}\right\rfloor$$$$^{∗}$$. If $$k$$ is not prime, write its prime factorization as $$k = $\prod p_i^{e_i}$$$, where $$p_i$$ are distinct prime factors and $$e_i$$ are their corresponding exponents. Then, $$$v_k(x!) = $\min\limits_i \left\lfloor \frac{v_{p_i}(x!)}{e_i}\right\rfloor.$$$$$

For any two positive integers $$a$$ and $$b$$, and any integer $$k$\geq 2$$$, the weight of the pair $$(a, b)$$ with respect to $$k$$, denoted by $$w_k(a, b)$$, is defined as $$$w_k(a, b) = \begin{cases}$\min(v_k(a!), v_k(b!)) & if v_k(a!)\neq v_k(b!);\\10^{100} & otherwise.\end{cases}$$$$

Next, define $$f_m(a, b)$$ as the minimum weight of the pair $$(a, b)$$ with respect to $$k$$, taken over all integers $$k$$ with $$2$\leq k\leq m$$$: $$$f_m(a, b)=$\min\limits_{2\leq k\leq m}w_k(a, b).$$$$

You are given two integers $$n$$ and $$m$$. Your task is to compute the sum of $$f_m(x, n)$$ over all positive integers $$x$$ less than $$n$$: $$$\sum_{1$\leq x\leq n - 1} f_m(x, n).$$$$

It can be shown that under the given constraints, the result is strictly less than $$10^{100}$$.

$$^{∗}$$$$\lfloor y\rfloor$$ denotes the floor of $$y$$, which is the greatest integer less than or equal to $$y$$.

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$t$$ ($$1 $\leq t \leq 100$$$). The description of the test cases follows.

The first and only line of each test case contains two integers $$n$$ and $$m$$ ($$2$\leq n\leq m\leq 10^7$$$) — the parameters of the function.

Note that there are no constraints on the sum of $$n, m$$ over all test cases.

For each test case, output a single integer representing $$\sum\limits_{1$\leq x\leq n - 1} f_m(x, n)$$$.

In the first test case, consider $$k = 3$\leq 5$$$:

Therefore, $$w_3(1, 3) = w_3(2, 3) = $\min(0, 1) = 0$$$. It can be shown that this is the minimum weight across all $$2$\leq k\leq 5$$$, so $$f_5(1, 3) = f_5(2, 3) = 0$$.

In the second test case, it can be shown that $$f_7(1, 6) = f_7(2, 6) = f_7(3, 6) = f_7(4, 6) = 0$$. For $$f_7(5, 6)$$, we consider $$k = 6$\leq 7$$$:

Therefore, $$w_6(5, 6) = $\min(1, 2) = 1$$$. It can be shown that this is the minimum weight across all $$2$\leq k\leq 7$$$, so $$f_7(5, 6) = 1$$.

Note: choosing $$k = 7 $\leq 7$$$ does not work, because $$v_7(5!) = v_7(6!) = 0$$, so $$w_7(5, 6) = 10^{100}$$.

In the third test case, it can be shown that $$f_{10}(1, 6) = f_{10}(2, 6) = f_{10}(3, 6) = f_{10}(4, 6) = 0$$. For $$f_{10}(5, 6)$$, we consider $$k = 9$\leq 10$$$:

Therefore, $$w_9(5, 6) = $\min(0, 1) = 0$$$. It can be shown that this is the minimum weight across all $$2$\leq k\leq 10$$$, so $$f_{10}(5, 6) = 0$$.
